name: Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate (Epsom salt)

structure.note: One formula unit; in the crystal six waters surround each Mg2+.

bonding.summary: Mg2+ ions wrapped in six water molecules, plus sulfate and one more water.
bonding.electronSharing: Magnesium gives two electrons to sulfate; water oxygens donate lone pairs toward Mg2+.

occurrence: Named after a bitter spring at Epsom, England.
facts: Magnesium sulfate is one of the main salts in seawater after sodium chloride.
summary: Epsom salt is a hydrated magnesium salt used in baths, farming and medicine.

name: Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate

structure.note: One formula unit; four waters bind directly to copper.

bonding.summary: Cu2+ ions surrounded by water molecules that donate lone pairs; sulfate balances the charge.
bonding.electronSharing: Water oxygens donate lone pairs into empty copper orbitals (coordinate bonds). Light absorbed by copper's d electrons gives the deep blue color.

uses: Testing for water (white anhydrous salt turns blue)
facts: Heating the blue crystals drives off the water, leaving a white powder that turns blue again when wet.
hazards: Harmful if swallowed; toxic to fish.
summary: Blue vitriol is a beautiful example of how water bound to metal ions creates color.

name: Potassium nitrate (saltpeter)

bonding.summary: K+ ions and flat nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium gives one electron to the nitrate group, whose three N–O bonds share a delocalized π pair.

occurrence: Cave and desert deposits; once scraped from manure heaps.
facts: Gunpowder burns because nitrate supplies its own oxygen; it decomposes above 400 °C.
summary: Saltpeter is the oxygen supplier in gunpowder and a valuable fertilizer.

name: Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda)

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hydrogen carbonate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives an electron to the HCO3 group, where the extra charge is shared by the two oxygens without hydrogen.

formation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl (Solvay process)
occurrence: The mineral nahcolite; mostly made by the Solvay process.
facts: Above about 50 °C it breaks down: 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, which makes cakes rise.
summary: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated or mixed with acid.

name: Sodium carbonate (washing soda)

bonding.summary: Two Na+ ions for each carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each sodium gives one electron; carbonate shares the two extra electrons over its three oxygens.

occurrence: Trona deposits and the Solvay process.
facts: Ancient Egyptians used natural soda (natron) to mummify bodies.
summary: Soda ash is a key ingredient of ordinary glass.

name: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach)

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hypochlorite ions with a Cl–O single bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium's electron ends up mostly on the oxygen of ClO−; chlorine is in the unusual +1 oxidation state, which makes it a strong oxidizer.

facts: Mixing bleach with acids releases chlorine gas; mixing it with ammonia releases toxic chloramines.
hazards: Corrosive; never mix with acids or ammonia.
summary: Household bleach is a dilute solution of sodium hypochlorite.

name: Lithium carbonate

bonding.summary: Two Li+ ions with one carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each lithium gives up its 2s electron to the carbonate group.

formation: 2 LiCl + Na2CO3 -> Li2CO3 + 2 NaCl (from salt-flat brines)
occurrence: Made from brines in salt flats and from spodumene ore.
facts: Its use for bipolar disorder was discovered by John Cade in 1949.
hazards: Toxic in overdose; doses must be monitored.
summary: Lithium carbonate is both a battery raw material and a psychiatric medicine.

name: Strontium nitrate (red fireworks)

bonding.summary: Sr2+ ions and two nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Strontium gives one electron to each nitrate. In a flame, excited strontium species emit red light.

facts: The red of fireworks comes mainly from SrOH and SrCl formed in the flame.
summary: Strontium nitrate makes the brilliant red in fireworks.

name: Potassium permanganate

bonding.summary: K+ ions and tetrahedral permanganate ions with Mn in its highest state, +7.
bonding.electronSharing: Manganese has given all seven valence electrons toward oxygen. Light pushes electrons from oxygen back toward manganese, which absorbs green-yellow light and makes the deep purple color.

formation: 2 MnO2 + 4 KOH + O2 -> 2 K2MnO4 + 2 H2O; then oxidized to KMnO4
facts: A few crystals turn a whole bucket of water purple; it decomposes at about 240 °C.
summary: Potassium permanganate is a vivid purple oxidizer used to clean water.

name: Potassium dichromate

structure.note: Two CrO4 tetrahedra sharing one oxygen, Cr–O–Cr 126°.

bonding.summary: Two chromium-oxygen tetrahedra joined through a shared oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Each chromium (+6) has given its six valence electrons toward oxygen. Charge transfer from oxygen to chromium absorbs blue light, giving the orange color.

uses: Old breathalyzers (orange turns green with alcohol)
facts: Early breathalyzers measured alcohol by how much orange dichromate turned green.
summary: Bright orange dichromate is a powerful oxidizer and a classic, but hazardous, lab reagent.
